A piano note has a pitch you could hum and a drum's thud has none because the piano's frequencies sit, very nearly, on whole-number multiples of one frequency and the drum's do not. This series explains where an instrument's frequencies come from with one piece of mathematics: they are read off the [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum) of an [operator](glossary.qmd#operator), the rule in the instrument's equation of motion. It works one instrument, the plucked string, completely, and then runs the same recipe on the others.

## The posts

1. [**What you hear**](../what-you-hear/index.qmd), with sounds and no differential equations: what makes a clear pitch, and what we hear as a sound's pitch, loudness, timbre and duration. A clear pitch means the [partials](glossary.qmd#partial) sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, so the sound nearly repeats at that rate.
2. [**One string, end to end**](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) works the plucked string completely: where its equation comes from, [from Newton's law](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#newton); why the sines are the right coordinates; why there is exactly one solution; how the motion becomes [the sound](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#sound); and [which conditions it used](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#conditions). A plucked string moves as a sum of shapes $\sin(n\pi x/L)$, each swinging at its own frequency $nc/2L$, because in the basis of sines, and only in a basis of [eigenfunctions](glossary.qmd#eigenfunction), the equation splits into independent springs.
3. [**Other instruments, same recipe**](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd) runs the string's recipe on a piano, a kalimba, a glockenspiel, drums, a bowed violin, a flute, a clarinet, a harmonica and a theremin, starting from an orchestra: each entry gives the problem, its spectrum, an animation and its sound, with the derivation of its equation in a fold.

**Beyond.** The appendix [*When does an equation have a spectrum?*](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd) gives the general theory for mathematical readers: when the solution of a differential equation is a sum over the spectrum of an operator, the deeper theory, and counterexamples, smallest first. Two further posts take up questions the answers raise: [*Can you hear the shape of a drum?*](../hear-the-shape-of-a-drum/index.qmd) and [*Did instruments shape our scales?*](../instruments-and-scales/index.qmd). [*A Piano*](../a-piano/index.qmd) is a playable upright with all 88 keys and its three pedals. Technical words link to the [glossary](glossary.qmd).

**Reading paths.** In order, 1 → 2 → 3, since each post uses the one before it. A listener can read 1 → 3, skipping post 3's folds; each entry links to the step of post 2 it reuses. A mathematician can read post 2, then the appendix.

## The series in one paragraph {#the-series-in-one-paragraph}

An instrument left to ring sounds a sum of decaying pure tones, one per mode:
$$
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\, e^{-t/\tau_k} \cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k).
$$
Here $p(t)$ is the air pressure at the listener; partial $k$ has frequency $f_k$, starting size $a_k$ and phase $\varphi_k$, and shrinks by a factor of $e \approx 2.7$ every $\tau_k$ seconds. This holds because a vibrating object of finite size whose motion is [linear](glossary.qmd#linear) and unchanging in time moves, left to itself, as a sum of [modes](glossary.qmd#mode), shapes that each oscillate at their own frequency and fade at their own rate, apart from the special cases [the appendix lists](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd#counterexamples). The body, the air and the room pass that motion on in a way that is also linear and unchanging in time, which keeps every $f_k$ and $\tau_k$, changes the amounts, and adds the filter's own ringing (the body's resonances, the room's reverberation).

The equation of motion, through its operator together with friction and radiation, fixes the $f_k$ and $\tau_k$; the playing, the radiation and where you listen fix the $a_k$. Pitch is heard mainly from where the $f_k$ sit; loudness from the sizes, weighted by frequency; timbre from all three lists, especially early on, plus noise that is not a mode; duration from the fading and from when the player stops or damps the note. Bowed and blown instruments are different: their motion is a single repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples, the resonator's modes shape which partials are strong, and the player sets loudness and duration. The series derives the $f_k$; the $\tau_k$ are mostly measured, and it says so where it uses them.

## Operator families and instrument classes {#operator-families-and-instrument-classes}

The [Hornbostel–Sachs classification](glossary.qmd#hornbostel-sachs), the scheme most used by those who study instruments, sorts them into five *classes* by what makes the sound;[^hs] this series groups them instead by [operator family](glossary.qmd#operator-family): instruments whose operators agree up to constants and how they are held, so that one calculation covers them all. The decimal codes in the first column are the scheme's.[^codes]

| Hornbostel–Sachs class | Instrument | Operator family: the rule, and how it is held | In the series |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| chordophone, 321.322 | violin, guitar | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$ on the string; ends tied | [2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) · [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#violin) |
| chordophone, 322 | harp | the same | [2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) |
| chordophone, 314.122 | piano | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$; ends pinned | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#piano) |
| aerophone, 421.121.12 | flute | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$ on the air's pressure; both ends open | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#flute) |
| aerophone, 422.211.2 | clarinet | the same; closed at the reed | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#clarinet) |
| aerophone, 412.132 | harmonica | $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$ on the reed; clamped and free | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#harmonica) |
| idiophone, 122.1 | kalimba | $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$; clamped and free | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#kalimba) |
| idiophone, 111.222 | glockenspiel | $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$; both ends free | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#glockenspiel) · [scales](../instruments-and-scales/index.qmd) |
| membranophone, 211.11 | timpani | $-c^2\Delta$ on a disk; rim fixed, air and kettle around it | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#drums) |
| membranophone, 211.212.1 | bass drum | $-c^2\Delta$ on a disk; rim fixed, a second head | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#drums) |
| electrophone, 531.1 | theremin | the number $1/LC$ | [3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#theremin) |

: Hornbostel–Sachs class, instrument, operator family, and where the series treats it: post 2 for the string, completely; post 3 for the others. {.striped}

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The decimal codes, and when electrophones were added</summary>

The numbers are the scheme's decimal codes, read from the left (Wikipedia, [Hornbostel–Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornbostel%E2%80%93Sachs), and the infoboxes of the instruments' articles). Among the chordophones (3), 321.322 are necked box lutes, such as the violin (bowed, 321.322-71) and the guitar; 322 are harps; 314.122 are board zithers with a resonator box, where the piano sits, as 314.122-4-8, sounded by hammers from a keyboard. Among the aerophones (4), 421.121.12 are open side-blown flutes with fingerholes; 422.211.2 are clarinets with a cylindrical bore and fingerholes; 412.132 are sets of free reeds, inside the interruptive free aerophones (412), where "the air-stream is interrupted periodically". Among the idiophones (1), 122.1 are plucked idiophones in the form of a comb, with laced-on lamellae (thin tongues), and 111.222 are sets of struck percussion plaques. Among the membranophones (2), 211.11 are single kettle drums and 211.212.1 single cylindrical drums with two heads. Number 531.1 places the theremin in 53, Sachs's group of radioelectric instruments, those that make their sound with electrically driven oscillators (Wikipedia, [Electronic musical instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_musical_instrument); for electric oscillators other than the theremin's coil and capacitor, [Relaxation oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relaxation_oscillator), [Voltage-controlled oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltage-controlled_oscillator) and [Hammond organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ)).

Hornbostel and Sachs published the scheme in 1914 with four classes (E. M. von Hornbostel and C. Sachs, "Systematik der Musikinstrumente: Ein Versuch", *Zeitschrift für Ethnologie* 46 (1914), 553–590, [archive.org](https://archive.org/details/zeitschriftfre46berluoft)); electrophones came later. Francis Galpin gave them a class of their own in his own scheme (F. W. Galpin, [*A Textbook of European Musical Instruments*](https://archive.org/details/textbookofeurope0000fran_n7q8), 1937, pp. 27–36), and Sachs added them to Hornbostel–Sachs as a fifth class, with the groups 51 to 53 (C. Sachs, [*The History of Musical Instruments*](https://archive.org/details/the_history_of_musical_instruments_curt_sachs), Norton, New York, 1940, pp. 447–467). Anthony Baines and Klaus Wachsmann's English translation keeps the four classes of 1914 (A. Baines and K. P. Wachsmann, "Classification of musical instruments", *The Galpin Society Journal* 14 (1961), 3–29, [doi:10.2307/842168](https://doi.org/10.2307/842168); D. Lee, ["Hornbostel-Sachs classification of musical instruments"](https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/22554/), *Knowledge Organization* 47 (2020), 72–91, for the electrophones' history and their absence from the translation).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>What varies inside one operator family</summary>

- **Strings and air columns**, $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$. What moves, the string's height or the air's pressure; the constants that set the lowest frequency, such as length, tension and mass per length; the ends, which are part of the operator: tied, open at both ends (flute) or closed at one (clarinet, pan pipes); and the playing: plucked (guitar, harp), bowed (violin) or blown.
- **Bending bars**, $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$. Steel tine, brass reed or metal bar; the ends, one clamped or both free, which change the frequency ratios; and the playing: plucked, struck or blown, which decides whether you hear the bar's own overtones or the whole-number multiples of a steady airflow.
- **Stiff strings**, $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$. The stiffness, whose effect is largest at the two ends of a piano's keyboard ([the piano in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#piano)).
- **Membranes**, $-c^2\Delta$. Tension and size, and what surrounds the head, which matters for timpani.
- **A single number**, such as $s/m$ for a mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $s$ or $1/LC$ for a coil and a capacitor (Wikipedia, [LC circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LC_circuit): Kirchhoff's law and $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$). Nothing varies but the number.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the classes and the mathematics part ways</summary>

Hornbostel–Sachs asks what makes the sound; the operator asks what oscillates and by what rule. Mostly the answers line up. Where they part:

- **The piano** is a chordophone, a board zither whose strings are struck by hammers, but its operator adds the bar's fourth derivative to the string's, $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$: its steel wire is stiff enough to bend like a bar ([the piano in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#piano)).
- **The harmonica** is an aerophone, classed by its interrupted airstream, though its reed is a clamped bar like the kalimba's tine. That agrees with [the harmonica in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#harmonica): the steady sound has only whole-number multiples of the puff rate, set by the chopped airflow, and the reed's own off-line overtones are absent from it.
- **The glockenspiel and the kalimba** are idiophones in different groups, struck and plucked, and in one operator family. They share the rule $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$, but their ends differ, both free for the glockenspiel bar and one clamped for the tine, so their operators differ, and so do their frequency ratios, $1 : 2.76 : 5.40$ against $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$.
- **A violin string and a flute's air column** are in different classes, yet their operators agree up to constants: both are $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$ with the value held at zero at both ends, the string's height at its tied ends and the air's extra pressure at the flute's open ends ([post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#flute)).
- **An electric guitar** is a chordophone with a pickup: its strings make the sound, and the electronics only pick it up and amplify it (Wikipedia, [Electric guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar)).
- **A theremin** is an electrophone: its two radio-frequency oscillators are coil-and-capacitor circuits, whose operator is the single number $1/LC$, with the player's hand as one plate of a capacitor and a mixer producing the audible difference (Wikipedia, [Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin)); [post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#theremin) derives it.

</details>
:::

## Did instrument makers know? {#did-instrument-makers-know}

Mostly not: makers found what works by trying and listening, and the theory explained it afterwards, often much later. Bell founders tuned each bell's partials by ear and lathe for the Zutphen carillon of 1644,[^zutphen] and experimenters found the laws of strings (Mersenne, 1636)[^mersenne] and the still points of a vibrating string (Noble and Pigot in the 1670s; Sauveur, 1701).[^nodes] The wave equation (d'Alembert, 1747),[^dalembert] modes and their superposition (Daniel Bernoulli, Euler, Fourier)[^modes] and the spectral theory behind this series (Sturm and Liouville, Rayleigh, Hilbert, Weyl)[^spectral] came after. Designing an instrument by computing its spectrum before it is made is recent: computed marimba bar profiles appear around 1990,[^orduna] and a bell with a major third was designed by finite-element computation in the 1980s.[^bell]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The longer story, with sources</summary>

**Instruments came first.** How Antonio Stradivari made his violins is not documented, so saying that he worked by trial and ear is an inference (Wikipedia, [Stradivarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius)). Bells show trial and ear at work more plainly. The blind Utrecht carillonneur Jacob van Eyck picked out the separate [partials](glossary.qmd#partial) of a bell by whistling at them, and held that a bell must be tuned after casting by changing its shape. In 1644 the city of Zutphen ordered a carillon from the founders Pieter and François Hemony, with van Eyck as its adviser. The brothers cast the bells slightly too thick, turned each on a lathe and shaved metal from the inside until its five principal partials were in tune. The Zutphen carillon is counted as the first tuned carillon (Wikipedia, [Jacob van Eyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_van_Eyck), drawing on L. Rombouts, [*Singing Bronze: A History of Carillon Music*](https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt15hvwrh), Leuven University Press, 2014, and B. Swager, [*A History of the Carillon*](https://www.allegrofuoco.com/carillon.html), DMus thesis, Indiana University, 1993; Wikipedia, [Zutphen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zutphen)).

**Laws from experiment.** The Pythagorean tradition tied consonant intervals to simple ratios of string lengths: half the length sounds an octave higher. In the late 1580s Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, hung weights on strings and found that tension works differently: an octave needs four times the weight and a fifth $9 : 4$, so the frequency goes with the square root of the tension ("July 2, 1591: Death of Vincenzo Galilei", [*APS News*, July 2015](https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2015/07/death-vincenzo-galilei), following S. Drake's dating of the experiments to 1588; W. B. Ashworth Jr., ["Vincenzo Galilei"](https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/vincenzo-galilei/), Scientist of the Day, Linda Hall Library, 2 July 2024). Marin Mersenne's [*Harmonie universelle*](https://imslp.org/wiki/Harmonie_universelle_(Mersenne,_Marin)) (1636) stated the laws of a string together: its frequency is inversely proportional to its length, proportional to the square root of its tension and inversely proportional to the square root of its mass per length, as in $f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}$ in [post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#sound) (Wikipedia, [Mersenne's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne%27s_laws)). In Oxford in the mid-1670s William Noble and Thomas Pigot found that a string can vibrate in parts with still points between them: small pieces of paper hung on the string stayed at rest at some points and trembled at others. John Wallis reported the discovery in the *Philosophical Transactions* in 1677 (J. Wallis, "Dr. Wallis's Letter to the Publisher, Concerning a New Musical Discovery; Written from Oxford, March 14. 1676/7", *Philosophical Transactions* 12 (1677), [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/stable/101761); Wikipedia, [Thomas Pigot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Pigot)). In 1701 Joseph Sauveur explained such motions to the Paris Academy: a string can vibrate at higher frequencies, which he called harmonics, separated by still points, which he called [nodes](glossary.qmd#node); both words are still in use (S. Dostrovsky, ["Sauveur, Joseph"](https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/sauveur-joseph), *Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography*).

**The mathematics, after the fact.** Brook Taylor (1713) worked out from mechanics the shape and the period of a string's simplest vibration (MacTutor, [Brook Taylor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Taylor/)). Jean le Rond d'Alembert (1747) wrote down the [wave equation](glossary.qmd#wave-equation) and solved it as two waves running in opposite directions (Wikipedia, [Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation)). Daniel Bernoulli (1753) stated that the general motion of a vibrating system is a [superposition](glossary.qmd#superposition) of its modes; Euler, d'Alembert and Lagrange did not accept that sums of sines could match an arbitrary starting shape (Wikipedia, [Daniel Bernoulli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Bernoulli), quoting L. Brillouin, [*Wave Propagation in Periodic Structures*](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.166889), 1946, for the 1753 statement). Leonhard Euler worked out the vibrations of a drumhead (L. Euler, "De motu vibratorio tympanorum", *Novi Commentarii academiae scientiarum Petropolitanae* 10 (1766), 243–260, [Euler Archive, E302](https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euler-works/302/)), and the functions now named after Bessel appear there for every whole-number order; the simplest, $J_0$, had already turned up in Daniel Bernoulli's hanging chain in the 1730s (R. C. Archibald, "Mathematicians and music", *American Mathematical Monthly* 31 (1924), 1–25, [part 3 on MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Archibald_music_3/), which also covers Taylor and d'Alembert; Wikipedia, [Bessel function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessel_function), history; D. D. Nolte, ["The ups and downs of the compound double pendulum"](https://galileo-unbound.blog/2020/10/18/the-ups-and-downs-of-the-compound-double-pendulum/), Galileo Unbound, 2020, for the hanging chain). Ernst Chladni (1787) made the [nodal lines](glossary.qmd#node) of vibrating plates visible with sand (Wikipedia, [Ernst Chladni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Chladni)). Joseph Fourier, in a memoir of 1807 and a book of 1822, argued that any function can be written as a sum of sines and cosines, and used such sums to solve the equation of heat flow (MacTutor, [Joseph Fourier](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Fourier/); Wikipedia, [Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series)). Charles Sturm and Joseph Liouville (1836–37) developed expansions of this kind for a whole class of second-order equations, the eigenvalue problems now named after them (MacTutor, [Charles Sturm](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Sturm/)). Karl Weierstrass (1858) corrected a conclusion of Lagrange, repeated by Laplace and others: they had held that two equal frequencies would make a small oscillation grow with time, and Weierstrass showed that for small oscillations about a stable rest they do not (K. Weierstrass, "Über ein die homogenen Functionen zweiten Grades betreffendes Theorem, nebst Anwendung desselben auf die Theorie der kleinen Schwingungen", *Monatsberichte der Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin* (1858), 207–220, [reprint in *Mathematische Werke* 1](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139567787.013); F. Brechenmacher, "L'identité algébrique d'une pratique portée par la discussion sur l'équation à l'aide de laquelle on détermine les inégalités séculaires des planètes (1766–1874)", [arXiv:0704.2931](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.2931), which quotes Lagrange (1766) and Weierstrass's correction). Lord Rayleigh's [*The Theory of Sound*](https://archive.org/details/theorysound06raylgoog) (1877) gathered the subject into one treatise (MacTutor, [Lord Rayleigh](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Rayleigh/)). David Hilbert's work on integral equations in the 1900s introduced the name *spectral theory* (MacTutor, [David Hilbert](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Hilbert/); Wikipedia, [Spectral theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory)), and Hermann Weyl (1911) proved that the frequencies of a drum determine its area (Wikipedia, [Weyl law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law); [*Can you hear the shape of a drum?*](../hear-the-shape-of-a-drum/index.qmd)).

**Computed design is recent.** A marimba bar is thinned by an arch cut under its middle. The arch lowers the lowest frequency more than the overtones, and so moves the first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, the uniform bar of [*Did instruments shape our scales?*](../instruments-and-scales/index.qmd), up to a whole-number multiple, usually 4 (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, [*The Physics of Musical Instruments*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21603-4), 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 19). Makers such as J. C. Deagan's company in Chicago, building marimbas from the early 1900s, and later Clair Omar Musser's, tuned each bar by grinding the arch and checking the result, by ear and with pitch-measuring devices as they appeared, such as Deagan's own "Deagan-o-meter" (1915) and the strobe tuner (1936); the shape of the arch was found by trial (Percussive Arts Society, [Hall of Fame: John Calhoun Deagan](https://pas.org/john-calhoun-deagan); "Chicago shop plays key role in keeping world's ensembles in tune", [WTTW News, 2016](https://news.wttw.com/2016/11/14/chicago-shop-plays-key-role-keeping-world-s-ensembles-tune); Wikipedia, [Clair Omar Musser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clair_Omar_Musser) and [Electronic tuner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_tuner), for the first strobe tuner, Conn, 1936). Bar profiles computed in advance, before any wood or metal is cut, appear in the acoustics literature around 1990 (F. Orduña-Bustamante, "Nonuniform beams with harmonically related overtones for use in percussion instruments", *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 90 (1991), 2935–2941, [doi:10.1121/1.401768](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.401768)). Bells followed the same path. A traditional tuned bell has a minor third among its main partials. In the 1980s engineers at the Eindhoven University of Technology designed a bell with a major third instead, by finite-element computation and structural optimization, and the Eijsbouts bell foundry cast it (A. Schoofs, F. van Asperen, P. Maas and A. Lehr, "Computation of bell profiles using structural optimization", *Music Perception* 4 (1987), 245–254, [doi:10.2307/40285368](https://doi.org/10.2307/40285368); Wikipedia, [Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell), section "Major third bell").

</details>
:::
